children.text: Built in 1830, this bahay na bato in Vigan was home, over generations, to the family of Alicia Syquia, wife of Elpidio Quirino, who later became the sixth President of the Philippines. Today it is a museum with furniture, paintings and exhibits on Quirino.

Syquia Mansion is a stone house (bahay na bato) on Quirino Boulevard in Vigan, a UNESCO World Heritage city. Justo Angco, a wealthy businessman of Chinese descent, began building it in 1830, and in 1875 it passed to the Syquia family as a dowry when his daughter married Gregorio Syquia. That is why the house carries the Syquia name rather than that of its builder. Wikipedia describes it as one of the oldest bahay na bato in Vigan. The Syquias descended from the Chinese Sy Kia family, who adopted the Spanish-style surname, and the family fortune is said to have come from Gregorio's involvement in the galleon trade between Acapulco and Manila. As the family grew and prospered, rooms and wings were added, and more rooms and fixtures were added again in Alicia's time.

The house is famous because Gregorio's granddaughter Alicia married Elpidio Quirino, the future president. The couple stayed here in 1921, when Quirino was a congressman, and after he became president he used the house as a retreat. Quirino is said to have held Cabinet meetings here, earning it the nickname "Malacañang of the North" (Malacañang is the presidential palace in Manila). The house received historical markers from the Philippine Historical Committee in 1950-1951 (English and Spanish markers) and a Heritage House marker from the National Historical Institute (NHI) in 2002. Alicia was killed along with three of her children by Japanese forces during the Battle of Manila in 1945. Two children are said to have survived, but a descendant has corrected details such as the children's names, so accounts you hear on tour may differ by source.

The building follows the classic bahay na bato plan: the ground floor is built of stone, brick and mortar, and the upper floor is timber. The ground floor was originally a garage for carriages (calesas), and the living quarters are upstairs. If you expect a grand Manila mansion, the first impression is modest, but once you climb to the second-floor living room you find thick hardwood plank floors, glass chandeliers and drapes decorated with capiz shells, a glimpse of how the old elite lived. A small peephole let the owners look over visitors below before letting them up, and a narrow corridor between the inner and outer walls let servants move around without entering the rooms unless summoned. The layout reflects the class divisions and security concerns of the time.

After the last occupant died in 1992 the house began to decay, and it was restored with funding from the National Historical Institute (now the National Historical Commission of the Philippines, NHCP), on condition that it be opened to the public. The July 2022 Luzon earthquake damaged some walls and windows, so check locally what is currently open before you go. Unlike the busier Calle Crisologo, it is quiet, a good place to pause and read some history during a Vigan trip.

The ground floor was originally where carriages were kept, so a carriage greets visitors as they enter. The cool walls of stacked stone and brick and the back-yard well, no longer in use, hint at the scale of 19th-century household life.

blocks.title: Second-floor living room and hardwood floors

children.text: The living room, with its thick hardwood floors, glass chandeliers and curtains decorated with capiz shells, is the highlight. Several parlors with chairs, paintings and busts follow one another.

blocks.title: Replica of Juan Luna's Spoliarium and Amorsolo paintings

children.text: The exhibits are said to include a replica of Juan Luna's masterpiece Spoliarium and three paintings by Fernando Amorsolo, regarded as the first National Artist for painting. The replica has darkened with age but stands out for its size.

The second-floor living room has a small peephole for checking on guests, and a passage between the walls let servants move about without passing through the rooms. Class and security are built right into the structure of the house.
The bedroom holds a four-poster bed ("Kama ni Ah-tay") made by the Chinese furniture maker Eduardo Ah-tay. It was once a status symbol and shows how wealthy the Syquia family was.
Woven cloth fans hang from the dining-room ceiling; before electricity, servants pulled them by hand to move the air. Small openings near the floor (ventanillas) let air circulate.

A large portrait of President Quirino hangs in the lobby, and the house also displays photographs of the Syquia and Quirino families and kitchenware collected from around the world. Alicia Syquia died in 1945 during the Battle of Manila in World War II, together with three of her children. Quirino was born in Vigan in 1890 and served as the sixth President of the Philippines. Knowing that story gives even ordinary pieces of furniture some meaning.

blocks.title: The azotea and the guided tour

children.text: The azotea, the central courtyard on the second floor, also served as a work area. A guide explains the layout and the anecdotes, so the visit is far more rewarding if you can join a tour. The guide is sometimes a descendant of the family, and some visitors have reported that no guide was available on the day.

items.title: Half-day Vigan route
items.subtitle: Syquia Mansion and the old town

children.text: Walk about
10 minutes
from your guesthouse in Vigan's old town to Syquia Mansion. The sun is gentler in the morning and there are fewer visitors.
See the carriage and the well at the entrance, pay the admission fee, then ask whether a guide is available. There are days without one, so allow some spare time.
Go upstairs and tour the living room, dining room, bedroom and azotea in that order. The peephole and the servants' corridor are easy to miss, so ask your guide.
Leave the mansion and stroll toward Calle Crisologo and Plaza Salcedo in
Vigan
, browsing other museums and shops on the way.
Have lunch at an old-town restaurant with Ilocano food such as Vigan longganisa and empanada.
The mansion itself takes about an hour. There is reportedly a lunch closure between 12:00 and 1:30 p.m., so early morning or late afternoon is recommended.

items.title: Full-day Vigan route
items.subtitle: From the mansion to the old town and the pottery village

children.text: Start with Syquia Mansion. Allow about
1 hour
Continue to nearby heritage sites such as the Crisologo Museum and the Bantay Watch Tower. Opening hours differ by site, so check.
Have lunch at a restaurant serving Ilocano food, such as The Hidden Garden.
Watch jars being made at the Pagburnayan pottery village.
Return to Calle Crisologo to walk the street at dusk and have dinner.
All of these places are in or near Vigan's old town and can be linked on foot or by tricycle.
Allow about
8–10 hours
by coach from Manila to Vigan (the operator lists 8–10 hours; a 2026 travel guide says 7–9). The
official Viron Transit route listing
shows fares from
one way. Confirm the terminal and seat class when booking.
By air, Philippine Airlines and Cebu Pacific fly from Manila to Laoag (LAO). From Laoag to Vigan by bus or van takes about
2 hours
or more.
Flights and bus routes change often, so check the latest announcements.
From Vigan's old town the mansion is about
10 minutes
on foot, close to Calle Crisologo and Plaza Salcedo.
When it is hot, take a tricycle or a calesa (horse-drawn carriage) and say "Syquia Mansion." Agree on the fare before you ride.
Vigan, in Ilocos, has a dry season from November to May, which is good for walking the old town. Inside the stone-and-timber house it tends to be cooler than outdoors even at midday.
The mansion is mostly an indoor visit, so it also fits a rainy day. However, it may close during heavy rain or a typhoon, so check first.

The mansion sits at the edge of the old town, so a boutique hotel in a restored old house around Calle Crisologo and Plaza Salcedo is convenient. It is within walking distance and the old town is lovely in the evening. Book early for the peak months of December–February and for holidays.

Ilocano dishes such as Vigan longganisa (small garlic sausage), Vigan empanada and okoy are famous. Restaurants around Calle Crisologo often tailor their menus to tourists, and prices vary by place, so check the menu.

A mansion visit is short, so we recommend fitting it into a stay of one night or more in Vigan, walking the whole old town. Because Vigan is a UNESCO World Heritage city, linking the mansion with churches, museums and the pottery village helps you understand both the layout of a Spanish colonial town and the life of Ilocano people. With children, you can keep them engaged by having them look for the servants' corridor and the peephole.
Ask before you enter whether a guide is available. With a guide you can hear about structural details such as the hidden peephole and passage.
The
mansion’s official visitor page
lists exhibition hours as 9 a.m.–noon and 1:30–4:30 p.m. The mansion closes on Tuesdays.
Weekdays are less crowded and let you take your time.
The admission fee is small, so carry some change.
The second-floor planks are old timber. Walk carefully and follow the signs.
Ask on site which areas you may photograph.
Combining Calle Crisologo, Plaza Salcedo and the Crisologo Museum makes a one-day old-town itinerary.
Check opening hours and fees in advance by phone (077 674 1643) or on the Syquia Mansion Facebook page.
Opening hours, fees and closing days differ by source and change often, and there are reports of the house being closed. Checking locally before you visit is essential.
The 2022 earthquake damaged some walls and windows, so some areas may be restricted.
Plan around the midday break and Tuesday closure. Check holiday notices for your date.
It is an old timber upper floor, so do not run or lean on railings.
The old town is very hot at midday. Bring water and a hat.
Confirm the fare before riding a calesa or tricycle.
A cobblestone street about
10 minutes
on foot from the mansion, lined with Spanish colonial-style buildings and souvenir shops.
The central square of the old town, about
10 minutes
on foot from the mansion, with carriages and snack stalls. A good starting point for a walk around the old town.
Another history museum in the old town, easy to pair with the mansion for a day route. It is known for introducing a notable figure from Vigan and local history.
A kiln village that makes Vigan's traditional jars (burnay). You can watch the pottery-making process.
